strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored gap: existing user simulators for tool agents are almost exclusively agent-friendly, so both training and evaluation of multi-turn tool agents are biased toward cooperative settings. The paper makes a convincing case that reported agent performance is inflated by this bias.

The four behavior categories (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterances) are well-motivated by grounding in marketing research (Bitner et al., 1990; Reynolds & Harris, 2009), open-domain dialogue studies (MIDAS dialogue acts), and real-world LLM interaction logs (LMSYS, WildChat), rather than being ad hoc inventions.

The framework tackles a genuinely hard design constraint—exhibiting non-collaborative behavior while still reliably conveying all task-critical information—via modular components (information sharding, dialogue state tracker, ending verifier, goal alignment verification), which is a sensible and reusable architecture.

Comprehensive evaluation across two distinct benchmarks (MultiWOZ with a newly built execution environment, τ-bench) and five agent LLMs, with per-behavior failure mechanism analyses (helper API repetition loops, API result hallucination for Qwen3-235b, apology-induced negative feedback loops, API input parameter hallucination) that go beyond headline numbers and provide actionable insight.

The fine-tuning study (SFT on collaborative dialogues yields >90% SR on collaborative users but degrades on non-collaborative modes) is a valuable practical finding: collaborative-only SFT actively produces brittle agents.

The multi-behavior experiments (Table 2) and the IGA metric help disentangle genuine behavioral challenge from simulator failures to communicate goals; the comparison against the prompt-only PBUS baseline shows the modular approach induces substantially more degradation while maintaining comparable IGA.
Human evaluation with 9 annotators on 180 dialogues with randomized position bias adds realism validation, and the paper is honest about mixed results (PBUS wins in tangential mode).
Extensibility is demonstrated concretely by porting the simulator from MultiWOZ to τ-bench 'with minimal effort,' and all prompts are released in the appendix.
weaknesses: Circularity and simulator dependence: the user simulator is built almost entirely from GPT-4.1-mini/GPT-4o-mini modules (state tracker, ending verifier, complaint/failure classifiers, style transfer), and goal alignment is verified by GPT-4o-mini. Degradation measured this way partly reflects the idiosyncrasies of one model family acting as simulator, and there is no ablation of how simulator-module model choice affects results.

The impatience mode is confounded with agent competence: triggers depend on the agent actually failing or delaying, so weaker models receive more impatience events by construction, and cross-model comparisons under impatience are not controlled. The paper acknowledges impatience causes less degradation but does not fully address this confound.

Regenerating simulations until goal alignment passes (C.3) introduces selection bias: simulations that align are re-sampled until success, potentially filtering out harder or more degenerate non-collaborative dialogues in a way that differs between the proposed simulator and PBUS.

Statistical rigor is limited: 89 MultiWOZ scenarios x 4 trials and 157 τ-bench scenarios x 4 trials, with no confidence intervals or significance tests. Small differences (e.g., GPT-4.1-mini 45.5 vs. 45.4, or Qwen3-30b-a3b relative SR of 107.9) are interpreted narratively though they are likely within noise.

Human evaluation is small (30 scenarios, 3 annotators per pair, 9 total) and shows mixed outcomes: the simulator significantly underperforms PBUS in tangential mode (largely due to truncated tangential + incomplete combinations), and only ~60% win rate on combined behaviors. The paper's claim that the simulator produces realistic behavior 'comparable to or exceeding PBUS' is stronger than the evidence supports.

Novelty is moderate: the contribution is largely a well-engineered prompt/module pipeline on top of the τ-bench user simulator (Yao et al., 2024) and ideas from Laban et al. (2025) and Luo et al. (2024), rather than a new method; the baseline comparison set is narrow (only PBUS, no other adversarial/robustness-oriented simulator baselines).

Some design choices may inflate degradation relative to realistic user behavior: e.g., the probabilistic anger escalation, permanent cynical tone after one outburst, and guaranteed complaint generation when tangential content is ignored (checked by another LLM module) could over-stress agents relative to natural user populations; the behavioral frequency/distribution of non-collaborative behaviors in the wild is not characterized.

Reproducibility concerns: many stochastic components (random persona sampling from Persona Hub, random dialogue act sampling, random truncation points, few-shot exemplar sampling) with limited discussion of seeds/controllability; the new MultiWOZ environment is described but the paper does not clearly commit to releasing the code and environments.

Scope limitations are under-discussed: only ReAct-style agents are evaluated; the taxonomy is defined for English, booking-centric tasks; and behavior categories are manipulated in isolation or fixed pairs rather than sampled from realistic distributions.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored gap: existing tool-agent user simulators (e.g., in tau-bench) overwhelmingly model cooperative users, and stress-testing agents against non-collaborative behaviors is practically relevant for robustness evaluation.

The four behavior categories (unavailable services, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterances) are grounded in prior service-marketing and open-domain dialogue literature, giving the taxonomy some external motivation rather than being purely invented.

The framework includes mechanisms to preserve goal alignment (information sharding, dialogue state tracker, ending verifier), and the Initial Goal Alignment (IGA) metric helps support the claim that performance drops stem from the challenging behaviors rather than simulator failures to convey task goals.

Evaluation is fairly broad in coverage: five agent LLMs across two benchmarks (MultiWOZ and tau-bench), single and combined behavior modes, quantified error analyses (duplicated helper API calls, API result hallucinations, apology rates, parameter hallucinations), a fine-tuning study showing SFT on collaborative data does not transfer robustness, and a pairwise human evaluation against a prompt-only baseline (PBUS).
Detailed appendices with all prompts, environment construction details, and error taxonomies support reproducibility and extensibility of the framework to other benchmarks.
weaknesses: Heavy circularity risk in the evaluation pipeline: the same class of LLMs (GPT-4.1-mini / GPT-4o-mini) serves as the user simulator, the dialogue state tracker, the ending verifier, and the Goal Alignment judge. Errors or biases in this LLM stack could systematically affect which simulations are counted and how 'success' is measured, and the paper provides no independent validation of the GA/tracker/verifier components against human annotation.

Limited statistical power and no significance testing: 89 MultiWOZ scenarios (restricted to multi-domain 'book' tasks) and 157 tau-bench scenarios with only 4 trials each; anomalies such as GPT-4.1-nano's relative SR exceeding 100% (113.1 under Impatience) and Qwen3-30b-a3b reaching 107.9 under Incomplete Utterances on tau-bench suggest high variance, yet no confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported.

Selection bias from the regeneration procedure: simulations failing goal alignment are regenerated until GA passes (C.3). This conditions the reported success rates on the subset of dialogues where the (LLM-based) tracker deemed all information delivered, which may distort the difficulty distribution and interact with the very failure modes under study.

Moderate conceptual novelty: the contribution is largely a suite of prompt-engineered LLM modules layered on the existing tau-bench simulation framework of Yao et al. (2024), drawing the taxonomy from prior literature; the architecture is engineering-heavy rather than a new technical method.

The PBUS baseline is a deliberately weak, naive prompt-only variant; there is no comparison against stronger existing simulators (e.g., trained/verifier-based simulators such as Luo et al. 2024 or Mehri et al. 2025), so claims that the framework 'outperforms simpler approaches' are only established against the easiest baseline.

The headline finding—that LLM agents degrade under off-distribution, adversarial user behaviors—is largely expected, and some analyses (e.g., model size vs. robustness) end in inconclusive 'mixed results' without actionable insight.

The human evaluation shows mixed outcomes: the proposed simulator loses to PBUS in the tangential mode, and it wins only ~60% on combined behaviors with 9 annotators and 30 scenarios per combination; the paper's framing of this as confirmation is somewhat generous.

The custom MultiWOZ agent environment is newly built by the authors with self-defined helper APIs and success criteria, so reported SRs are not comparable to any prior results and the environment itself is never validated against existing MultiWOZ-based agent setups.

Several design choices are heuristic and under-motivated (e.g., fixed initial anger probability of 0.5 with +0.1 increments, 'three levels of anger', 3 generated unavailable goals per scenario), and the sensitivity of results to these hyperparameters is unexamined.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing user simulators for tool agents are almost exclusively collaborative, and this paper provides the first systematic framework for simulating non-collaborative behaviors (unavailable services, tangential chat, impatience, incomplete utterances) in tool-agent settings.

The taxonomy is well-grounded, drawing on service-encounter marketing research (Bitner et al.; Reynolds & Harris), open-domain dialogue act schemes (MIDAS), and empirical patterns from real user-agent data (LMSYS, WildChat), rather than being purely ad hoc.

The simulator design carefully handles a key technical challenge—goal alignment under non-collaborative behavior—via information sharding, a dialogue state tracker, and an ending verifier, and this is validated with a dedicated Initial Goal Alignment metric plus a regeneration procedure.

Evaluation is broad: five agent LLMs (closed- and open-source), two benchmarks with distinct characteristics, four trials per scenario, quantified error analyses (helper-API duplication, API hallucination, apology ratios, complaint counts), ablations on multiple concurrent behaviors, and a human evaluation against a prompt-only baseline.

The fine-tuning study is a valuable addition: it shows that SFT on collaborative-only data yields agents that perform well collaboratively but remain vulnerable to non-collaborative users, supporting the paper's claim that current agent evaluations overestimate real-world robustness.
Extensive appendix (all prompts, environment construction, human evaluation protocol, dialogue examples) supports reproducibility and extension to other benchmarks.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the framework is largely an assembly of prompt-based LLM modules layered on top of the existing τ-bench simulator (Yao et al., 2024), with the goal-alignment machinery explicitly inspired by prior work (Laban et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024). The four behavior types are induced via heuristics and prompt engineering rather than a new methodological contribution.

Potential circularity in evaluation: GPT-4o-mini both drives/verifies goal alignment of the simulator and is from the same family as the simulator LLM (GPT-4.1-mini). GA/IGA reliability is not validated against human judgment, so it is possible that some agent 'failures' partly stem from simulator artifacts rather than genuine user difficulty.

Internal inconsistencies weaken confidence: the text states Qwen3-235b-a22b shows 'substantial degradation (30.2% relative SR)' for unavailable service, but Table 1 reports 80.2%; GPT-4.1-nano's impatience relative SR (113.1) exceeds 100% without explanation; some reported aggregates (e.g., 'average drop of 29.1%') are hard to reconcile with the tables.

The main baseline (PBUS) is weak—a prompt-only augmentation of the same simulator. The human evaluation is mixed, with the proposed simulator losing to PBUS in the tangential mode, which somewhat undercuts the claim of superior realism.

Limited scope of evaluation: only the ReAct agent scaffold is tested; the MultiWOZ subset is small (89 'book'-only scenarios); and τ-bench scenarios where human transfer is the intended solution were excluded, which may bias measured degradation (agents legitimately offloading difficult users would otherwise count as success).

Several behaviors (impatience complaints, tangential-related complaints) consume agent reasoning turns, so part of the measured degradation may reflect budget exhaustion interacting with the simulator's escalation mechanics rather than intrinsic agent fragility; the analysis acknowledges but does not fully disentangle this.

Writing quality needs polishing: numerous typos and grammatical issues ('perfer', 'reataurant', 'reservate', 'Incomple Utterance', 'dialolgue') appear even in figures and tables, and Figures 1–3 are dense and hard to parse.

strengths: Addresses a real and underexplored gap: existing user simulators for tool agents are overly cooperative, and this paper provides a systematic framework for stress-testing agents against non-collaborative behaviors.

The four-behavior taxonomy (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterance) is grounded in marketing/service-encounter literature and real user-LLM conversation data, with the derivation process transparently documented in the appendix.

Comprehensive experimental design: two benchmarks with different characteristics (MultiWOZ, τ-bench), five agent models, single and combined behavior modes, fine-tuning experiments (collaborative-only vs. mixed data), and extensibility demonstrations on ColBench and MINT.

Beyond aggregate numbers, the paper provides insightful behavior-specific failure analyses (helper API repetition loops, API result hallucinations by Qwen3-235b, counterproductive apology loops under impatience), which are actionable for agent development.

The goal-alignment mechanism (information sharding + dialogue state tracker + ending verifier) with GA/IGA verification and human-correlation check (MCC 0.77) addresses the key validity concern that degradation stems from simulator failure rather than genuine difficulty.

Extensive appendices with all prompts, error taxonomies, step-limit ablations (50 vs. 30 steps), and excluded-case analyses support reproducibility and show the authors anticipated confounds (e.g., reasoning-step limits, human-transfer gaming).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework is essentially a pipeline of prompted GPT-4.1-mini/4o-mini modules layered on top of the existing τ-bench simulator (Yao et al., 2024) plus techniques borrowed from prior work (Laban et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024). The contribution is more of a well-executed engineering/benchmarking effort than a methodological advance.

The taxonomy is defined by author-driven clustering of literature-identified behaviors; there is no empirical validation that these four categories are the most representative or that the taxonomy is exhaustive (e.g., no comparison against real logged user-agent dialogues at scale).

Some headline findings are relatively expected (agents degrade when users behave adversarially or provide underspecified input, echoing known multi-turn fragility results such as Laban et al., 2025), which weakens the significance of the main empirical claim for strong models — GPT-4.1-mini shows almost no degradation (95-99% relative SR).

Evaluation rigor concerns: success rates averaged over only 4 trials on small test sets (89 MultiWOZ, 157 τ-bench scenarios) with no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; several reported differences (e.g., impatience vs. collaborative for GPT-4.1-mini) are likely within noise.

Modifying τ-bench by removing transfer_to_human, and regenerating simulations until goal alignment passes, both alter the standard benchmark setup; the GA judge itself was validated against only one annotator on 40 dialogues.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4.1-mini as the user simulator raises concerns about simulator-model-specific artifacts; no analysis of how simulator choice affects conclusions, and cost/latency of the multi-module pipeline (state tracker + verifiers per turn) is not reported.

The fine-tuning-with-non-collaborative-data experiment (§D.7) is a small addendum on one model with one dataset size; given the paper's motivation that robustness matters, this direction deserves more depth (e.g., scaling curves, generalization across benchmarks).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing user simulators for tool agents are agent-friendly, and stress-testing agents against non-collaborative users is practically relevant

Comprehensive experimental coverage: two benchmarks (MultiWOZ and τ-bench), five agent LLMs, four behavior modes plus combined modes, fine-tuning studies, and cross-domain extensibility checks (ColBench, MINT)

Thoughtful analysis of behavior-specific failure mechanisms (helper API repetition, API-result hallucination, apology-induced negative feedback loops), which goes beyond just reporting aggregate degradation

Attention to evaluation validity: goal-alignment verification with regeneration, reasoning-step-limit ablations, human correlation check for the judge model (MCC 0.77), and pairwise human evaluation against a prompt-only baseline
Appendix is unusually thorough (prompts, error taxonomies, excluded-case analyses), supporting reproducibility once code/data are released
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially a collection of prompt-engineered LLM modules layered on the existing τ-bench user simulator; the four-behavior taxonomy arises from a heuristic clustering of marketing literature rather than a validated empirical study, and each module is ad hoc rather than a principled framework

The regeneration-until-goal-aligned protocol introduces selection bias: simulations are re-run until the agent receives a solvable configuration, and the authors' own audit shows 49% of flagged misalignments were checker errors; the resulting test distribution may favor easier dialogues, and success rates are computed on this filtered set without quantifying how regeneration shifts difficulty

Small and narrow evaluation sets: only 89 MultiWOZ scenarios restricted to multi-domain 'book' tasks with 4 trials each, producing noisy cells (e.g., several relative-SR values above 100%, such as GPT-4.1-nano at 113.1% under impatience and Qwen3-30b-a3b at 107.9% under incomplete utterance) that undermine confidence in behavior-specific conclusions

Weak baseline: the main simulator comparison (PBUS) is a simple prompt-only strawman; no comparison against stronger goal-tracking simulators (e.g., trained or verifier-based simulators cited in related work), leaving the claimed architectural advantage under-supported

Claim of testing 'state-of-the-art tool agents' is overstated: the strongest evaluated agent is GPT-4.1-mini; leading reasoning/agentic models commonly used in τ-bench-style evaluations are absent, so the severity of degradation may be misestimated

Some mode definitions are environment-dependent and arguably unfair: impatience is triggered whenever the agent has not resolved the goal after all information is provided, which can punish legitimate multi-step reasoning; the unavailable-service mode is defined relative to a specific API surface, limiting generalizability of the reported degradation
Potential circularity: GPT-4.1-mini serves both as the simulator backbone (and in several LLM modules) and as an evaluated agent, which may interact with the analysis of model-specific failure modes

Human evaluation is small-scale (9 annotators, 30 sampled scenarios per setting) and only compares against the weak baseline; some combined modes are admitted to be unnatural, raising questions about the ecological validity of the multiple-behavior results
Fine-tuning findings are only on MultiWOZ with three small models and a single training recipe, so the practical claims about fine-tuning-induced fragility are preliminary

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing user simulators for tool agents are agent-friendly, and testing/training against non-collaborative users is an important, underexplored direction with practical significance for robustness evaluation.

The four-behavior taxonomy (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterances) is grounded in marketing/service research, open-domain dialogue literature, and real user-LLM data (LMSYS, WildChat), with the derivation process transparently documented in Appendix A rather than asserted ad hoc.

Careful simulator design addressing a real failure mode of non-collaborative simulation: goal alignment is enforced via information sharding, a dialogue state tracker, and an ending verifier, so increased difficulty is not confounded with unsolvable dialogues. The goal-alignment metric, its failure analysis, and a human correlation check (MCC 0.77) are reported.

Comprehensive evaluation: five agent models across two benchmarks (MultiWOZ and tau-bench), combined behaviors, extensibility experiments on ColBench and MINT, fine-tuning studies showing that models trained on collaborative data remain vulnerable (and that training on non-collaborative data helps), plus detailed error analyses (helper API repetition, API result hallucination, apology loops, parameter hallucination) that yield actionable insights.

Human evaluation with nine annotators comparing against a prompt-only baseline (PBUS), supporting both difficulty and realism claims; the simulator is positioned as an extensible framework rather than a one-off benchmark, and code/data release is promised.

The paper is honest about scope choices (excluded retrieval tasks, excluded human-transfer scenarios) and justifies them with data and additional experiments (e.g., 50-step limit verification, merged single-domain results).
weaknesses: Headline results are mixed: the strongest agent (GPT-4.1-mini) degrades only mildly (e.g., 95-99% relative SR on MultiWOZ), so the claim that 'state-of-the-art tool agents exhibit significant performance degradation' is driven largely by weaker/smaller models; robustness conclusions partly rest on models like GPT-4.1-nano whose collaborative baseline is already low.

Comparison baseline (PBUS) is relatively weak as the only direct simulator comparison; the architectural contribution (LLM modules for state tracking, verifiers, complaint generators) is an engineering combination of existing ideas (Laban et al. information sharding, Yao et al. simulator backbone, Luo et al. verification), so the novelty is more in the problem framing and taxonomy than in the method itself.

Potential circularity/LLM-dependence: the simulator, goal-alignment judge, behavior classifiers, and several analyses all use GPT-family models, which could bias difficulty and evaluation; judge-model reliability is checked on only 40 sampled dialogues with a single annotator.

Evaluation scale is modest for the core benchmark: 89 MultiWOZ scenarios (book tasks only) and 157 tau-bench scenarios (with 8 excluded), 4 trials each; some per-condition analyses (e.g., combined-behavior modes, 8 human-transfer scenarios) have very small effective sample sizes.

Some reported numbers are noisy or awkwardly interpretable (e.g., relative SR of 113.1 for impatience, PBUS outperforming Ours on several combined modes in Table 2, higher collaborative SR for PBUS on tau-bench), which complicates the claim that the proposed simulator is uniformly superior; the argument leans on IGA and human eval rather than consistent SR wins.

Realism of behaviors is asserted via taxonomy grounding and a pairwise human study (~60% win rate), but there is no validation against real user-agent logs showing that the simulated behavior distributions match actual non-collaborative interactions; the impatience escalation mechanism (probabilistic anger increase, permanent cynicism) is heuristic.

Generalization experiments (MINT) show weaker or absent degradation patterns for some modes, and the paper's explanation for these differences is somewhat post-hoc; the practical impact of the fine-tuning recommendations is not validated beyond one 3B model.
